purpose: run the production databases so they stay available, correct, performant and recoverable, with changes made safely
entry_criteria: Databases and their owners are inventoried
procedure: Monitor availability, replication lag, connection use, disk growth, lock waits and slow queries, and alert on thresholds with runbook links.
Verify backups by restoring them into a test instance on a schedule and checking data and application connectivity; an untested backup is not a backup.
Tune with evidence: review the slowest and most frequent queries, check query plans, and add or remove indexes by measured effect.
Apply patches and schema changes through the change process, using online and backward-compatible migrations (expand then contract).
Manage access: named accounts, least privilege, rotated credentials and audited administrative access.
Rehearse failover and point-in-time recovery, record the actual recovery time and data loss against the objectives.
deliverables: tuning changes with before and after plans
acceptance_criteria: Restores are tested on a schedule
Measured recovery meets RPO and RTO or the gap is recorded
Administrative access is named and audited
validation_method: Database administrator and service owner review.

validation.command: pg_restore --list backup.dump | head   # example; then restore into a scratch instance and run row-count checks
validation.expect: restore completes and counts match the source

validation.command: psql -c "select now()-pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() as lag"   # example on a replica

failure_modes.detection: First restore attempt fails during an incident

failure_modes.response: Verify with the plan and drop it

worked_example: ILLUSTRATIVE: A monthly restore test brings the latest backup up in a scratch instance in 38 minutes against a 60-minute target, and row counts match; a column rename is done by adding the new column, backfilling in batches, switching reads, then dropping the old.
